title: Need an Idea for Tomorrow's Lesson Plan? Try a Quiz
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart makes the case for using a low-stakes oral and written quiz of five to ten questions as a strong default lesson-plan filler on any day, grounding the recommendation in retrieval-practice research. He cites findings that testing beats rereading or reteaching for long-term retention, that quizzes don't need to be comprehensive to boost recall of untested material, that testing produces a forward effect helping future learning, and that quizzing helps students distinguish true knowledge from mere familiarity, avoiding what he calls the Familiarity Trap. He offers three practical pointers: keep quizzes low-stakes by grading them as classwork rather than assessment, explicitly teach students why quizzing beats rereading so they buy into the practice, and recognize that the quizzing effect can come from many formats, not just a single quiz format.
points: Central research claim: taking a test on material beats rereading or reteaching it for long-term retention — Stuart cites this as the power of tests, a principle underlying his Principles of Learning Course.

Quizzes don't need to be comprehensive to help — testing on some material boosts recall of related untested material too, and produces a forward effect that helps students learn new related material later.
Keeping quizzes low-stakes, a classwork grade rather than an assessment grade, is essential to using them frequently without adding grading pressure or anxiety.
Quizzing helps students escape the Familiarity Trap, the tendency to mistake recognition for actual retrievable knowledge, which is a common and costly study misconception.
quotes: Here's a fair idea for tomorrow's lesson plan, regardless of what you teach: a low-stakes quiz. And I'm talking old school here: you ask the students 5-10 questions on what they've learned, and they answer the questions.
Reason 2: Even better, your quizzes don't need to be comprehensive. Tests even help with recall of untested material.
Reason 3: Testing doesn't just help with retaining information previously learned — it helps with retaining related information to be learned tomorrow. This is known as the forward effect of testing.
Reason 4: And finally, quizzes help a student see what they know versus what they are familiar with. In other words, a quiz gets students out of the Familiarity Trap.
